new.question: GPT-3 saw each training example fewer than once on average during its pretraining run. Why don't frontier labs simply train for many more passes through the same data?
new.answer: Models that revisit the same text too many times start memorizing it word-for-word instead of generalizing — and the next pass on internet-scale data costs millions in compute.
choices: Models that revisit the same text too many times start memorizing it word-for-word instead of generalizing — and the next pass on internet-scale data costs millions in compute.
Federal law caps every commercial language model at one training pass — additional passes require a special government license that labs cannot obtain.
GPU memory cannot physically hold the same example twice — a hardware lock erases each training file the moment the model has read it once.
The training data is leased from publishers by the hour — after the first pass the license expires and the lab loses access to the dataset entirely.
new.context: Frontier LLMs like GPT-3 train for less than one full epoch over their corpus. Two reasons push against more passes: overfitting (the model memorizes specific passages, which can hurt generalization and surface verbatim training data at inference) and cost (a single pass over a trillion-token corpus already costs tens of millions of dollars in compute; doubling that for marginal accuracy gain rarely pencils out).

new.question: When ChatGPT seems to be 'thinking' about your prompt and writing its reply, what is the model actually doing for every single word it produces?
new.answer: Predicting the most likely next piece of text given everything before it, then the next, then the next — that loop is the whole trick.
choices: Predicting the most likely next piece of text given everything before it, then the next, then the next — that loop is the whole trick.
Looking up the answer in a giant indexed database of human conversations — the model fetches the closest matching reply and copies it word-for-word.
Running an internal panel of smaller AI personalities that debate the response — the winning persona dictates the final wording sent to the user.
Generating the entire response in parallel as a single block of text — the model writes the conclusion first and then fills in the middle sentences.
new.context: A modern chatbot generates output one token at a time, autoregressively: at every step it produces a probability distribution over its vocabulary, samples a token from that distribution (or picks the most likely one), appends it to the running text, and feeds the new sequence back through the model for the next step. There is no search, no internal database of stored answers, and no parallel-generation shortcut. The mystique of 'reasoning' is built entirely from billions of next-token guesses.

new.question: Stability AI keeps releasing newer Stable Diffusion versions (1.5, 2.0, XL, 3, 3.5). The older versions still run on the same consumer GPU. Why does the company keep training new ones?
new.answer: Newer versions are trained on better-curated data and bigger compute budgets — they fix earlier failure modes like mangled hands and produce sharper images.
choices: Newer versions are trained on better-curated data and bigger compute budgets — they fix earlier failure modes like mangled hands and produce sharper images.
The older versions stop working after twelve months by design — a built-in expiration date forces users to download the newest release every year.
Each version is licensed to a different country exclusively — Stability must release new ones so other nations can have their own legal copy of the software.
The original training data is automatically deleted after each release — the lab must rebuild every version completely from scratch with no carryover.
new.context: Image generators improve along several axes between releases: training-data curation (filtering out low-quality or copyright-flagged images), compute scale (larger models with more parameters), architectural changes (Stable Diffusion 3 moved to a rectified-flow transformer architecture), and targeted fixes for known failure modes (early Stable Diffusion famously produced anatomically wrong hands). Each release is meant to be visibly better, not just rebranded.

new.question: In 2023, a Stanford team built 'Alpaca,' a chatbot trained for about $600. They did not train it from scratch. They started from Meta's Llama model and fine-tuned it on instruction-following examples. Why did this work?
new.answer: Llama had already learned grammar, common-sense reasoning, and world facts during its massive pretraining — Alpaca only had to teach it the chatbot-reply style on top.
choices: Llama had already learned grammar, common-sense reasoning, and world facts during its massive pretraining — Alpaca only had to teach it the chatbot-reply style on top.
The $600 figure was a public-relations estimate — the team actually spent roughly the same amount Meta spent training Llama itself, just disclosed differently.
Stanford had a private prototype of GPT-4 leaked through a partnership — Alpaca was a thin wrapper around that internal version with a renamed brand.
Llama runs on a magic compression chip that costs $600 to manufacture — the chip lets any small lab match frontier-lab capability for the same hardware price.
new.context: Stanford's Alpaca (March 2023) was a landmark demonstration of transfer learning. Researchers started from a pretrained Llama 7B and fine-tuned it on about 52,000 instruction-response pairs generated by GPT-3.5 (the 'self-instruct' technique). Total compute cost: about $600. The result behaved like ChatGPT on many tasks. The lesson generalized: once a base model has absorbed broad knowledge from internet-scale pretraining, the cost of teaching it a new skill is dramatically lower than building such capability from zero.

new.question: GPT-4 has hundreds of billions of parameters. ChatGPT serves millions of users at once, but the model itself isn't running continuously on every server. Where are all those parameters actually stored when nobody is using the model?
new.answer: On disk as a single enormous file — GPT-3's parameters at full precision weigh about 700 gigabytes, like a giant fixed lookup table that gets loaded into GPU memory when a request comes in.
choices: On disk as a single enormous file — GPT-3's parameters at full precision weigh about 700 gigabytes, like a giant fixed lookup table that gets loaded into GPU memory when a request comes in.
Encoded into the firmware of dedicated AI chips at the factory — each parameter is a separate transistor and you cannot run the model on hardware it wasn't burned into.
Distributed across users' devices like a torrent — every time you send a prompt your laptop downloads a slice of the parameters and contributes it back to the cluster.
Generated fresh on every request by a smaller seed program — the parameters are recomputed from scratch in milliseconds whenever a user types a new question.
new.context: Trained model weights are stored as plain files on disk. GPT-3's 175 billion parameters at 32-bit precision occupy about 700GB; at 16-bit precision (the more common deployment format) about 350GB. When a server needs to run inference, the file is loaded into the memory of the GPUs that will serve requests, and computations happen there. Parameters never change at inference time — they are a fixed lookup table burned in by training. Recognition skill: model size is a real physical artifact (a file), not an abstract description of capability.

new.question: A high-school student asks ChatGPT to write the code for a programming-class project. The code runs, the project gets an A. A year later the student tries to extend the project and discovers the variable names made no sense and the logic was wrong in two places. What's the realistic lesson?
new.answer: AI-generated code that runs is not the same as code you understand — you owe a careful read-through before turning it in, because tomorrow you will be the one stuck with it.
choices: AI-generated code that runs is not the same as code you understand — you owe a careful read-through before turning it in, because tomorrow you will be the one stuck with it.
AI-generated code is never wrong if it runs the first time — a working test result proves the code is logically correct and ready to be submitted for credit.
AI-generated code becomes the student's legal property automatically — no school can fairly grade work that the chatbot produced on the student's behalf.
AI-generated code is always written by stealing from open-source repositories — every project handed in this way is grounds for academic dishonesty proceedings.
new.context: Large language models are pattern-completion engines. They produce code that looks like working code from their training data, but they have no understanding of the specific problem being solved. The output often runs and even passes a graded rubric, while containing variable names that don't match the domain, logic that handles only the common path, or subtle bugs that don't trigger on the test input. The recognition skill: AI assistance shifts the cost of understanding the code from writing-time to maintenance-time. The student who didn't read the AI's output carefully is the same student who can't fix it a year later.

new.question: Sam Altman, OpenAI's CEO, said in 2024 that AGI was 'within reach.' He had been saying versions of that publicly since 2019. The capability bar has moved each time. Why does he keep saying it?
new.answer: Believable AGI-soon talk pulls in investors, talent, and government attention — OpenAI raised tens of billions over those years, much of it on the premise that the next big breakthrough was always one round away.
choices: Believable AGI-soon talk pulls in investors, talent, and government attention — OpenAI raised tens of billions over those years, much of it on the premise that the next big breakthrough was always one round away.
Altman is contractually required to declare AGI imminent every five years — OpenAI's nonprofit charter from 2015 includes a clause obligating the CEO to make this exact public statement.
He has solved AGI privately each time and announces it the same year — the public versions of the models you can use are deliberately weaker so that internal AGI stays unreleased.
Federal regulators classify CEOs who don't predict AGI as price-fixing colluders — the SEC mandates the prediction at every annual shareholder meeting.
new.context: Sam Altman has been publicly predicting that artificial general intelligence is close for years: 2019 ('AGI in a decade'), 2023 ('not very long'), 2024 ('within reach'). Each prediction repositions OpenAI as the company at the frontier, which helps in fundraising rounds, talent recruitment, and lobbying access. The recognition skill: when a CEO repeats a forecast for half a decade and the forecast keeps not arriving but the company keeps raising on it, the forecast is doing rhetorical work, regardless of whether it is also sincere.

new.question: Nearly every advanced AI chip in the world — including Nvidia's H100 and successors — is manufactured by a single company on a single island. Which company on which island, and why does that fact alarm Washington?
new.answer: TSMC, based in Taiwan, fabricates the bulk of frontier AI silicon — a Chinese blockade or invasion of Taiwan would freeze the global supply of leading-edge chips overnight.
choices: TSMC, based in Taiwan, fabricates the bulk of frontier AI silicon — a Chinese blockade or invasion of Taiwan would freeze the global supply of leading-edge chips overnight.
Foxconn, based in mainland China, assembles every Nvidia accelerator — the United States cannot ship any chip out of the country without Beijing's signed approval.
Samsung, based in South Korea, holds the patents on every transistor design — no other firm in the world can legally produce frontier silicon without Samsung's licence.
Intel, based in Arizona, fabricates the global supply singlehandedly — a wildfire or earthquake in the Phoenix area would knock out frontier AI production worldwide for years.
new.context: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) produces roughly 90% of the world's leading-edge logic chips, including the GPUs used to train and run frontier AI models. Nvidia designs the H100 and its successors but does not own a fab — TSMC builds them. This single-island concentration is the central fact behind the US CHIPS Act (2022), the Arizona TSMC fabs under construction, and Washington's anxiety about a Taiwan Strait crisis. Recognition skill: the bottleneck on AI capability is not the model weights, which can be copied. It is the physical fab that prints the silicon.
